Title: Do driving restrictions improve air quality: Take Beijing-Tianjin for example?
URL Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0048969719364046
Markdown Content:
The RDD is used to test whether the driving restriction improve air quality.
Tianjin and Beijing are selected as cases to study.
The daily data of air quality index and six kinds of pollutants are used.
To manage air quality, Tianjin introduced driving restriction (DR) in 2014 and new driving restriction (NDR) in 2018.
Ever since February 22th, 2018, private cars that belong to Beijing have been treated equally as local cars of Tianjin.
However, existing studies rarely compare the effects of driving restrictions in different cities.

In this paper, using the regression discontinuity design (RDD) model and urban air quality monitoring data from Beijing and Tianjin during the period 2014 to 2018, we explore whether driving restriction policies can improve air quality in Beijing and Tianjin.
The main results are as follows. (1) Our results of regression discontinuity design revealed that the DR had no obvious improvement in the air quality in Tianjin.

Furthermore, the effect of the DR decreases along with its implementation. (2) The implementation of the DR in Tianjin had slight improvement in air quality in Beijing, which mainly reduced emissions from cars.
In other words, the DR brought about weak externality. (3) We found that the effect of NDR on the air pollution was limited in both Tianjin and Beijing.
To sum up, we compared the NDR with DR and found out that the DR was more effective in the short run, while the NDR could work well in the long term.
As the motor vehicle ownership increasing rapidly, haze days in China appear more frequently.
At present, mobile source pollution has become an important source of air pollution (Yan, 2017；Chen et al., 2019a, Chen et al., 2019b, Chen et al., 2019c, Chen et al., 2019d).

In particular, the contribution of mobile sources to the concentration of fine particulate matter (PM 2.5) is as high as 10% to 50%, especially in megacity cities, such as Beijing, Shanghai and densely populated areas in the east.

In 2017, the total emission of four pollutants from motor vehicles nationwide was estimated to be 43.597 million tons, a 2.5% reduction from 2016, with 33.273 million tons of carbon monoxide, 4.071 million tons of hydrocarbons, 5.743 million tons of nitrogen oxides and 509 million tons of particulate matter (PM).

Scholars have found out that haze has a strong spatial spillover effect, and the joint prevention and control between cities should be considered (Ma and Zhang, 2014; Shao et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019a, Chen et al., 2019b, Chen et al., 2019c, Chen et al., 2019d).

In March 2017, Premier Keqiang Li delivered a report on the work of the government at the fifth session of the 12th National People's Congress that said: we will strengthen control over exhaust emitted by motor vehicles, and we will fight to win the battle of conserving energy, reducing emissions, and improving the environment.
On September 20, 2008, in order to alleviate the road traffic pressure and urban air pollution during the Olympic Games, license plate last number odd-and-even rule exercised on Beijing automobile.
Since October11, 2008, the vehicles have been restricted one out of five weekdays based upon the last numbers of their license plates.

On March 1, 2014, in order to effectively alleviate traffic congestion, reduce energy consumption and improve air environment quality, Tianjin began to implement driving restriction (DR) which restricted the vehicle tail number every day.
Based on coordinated development between Beijing, Tianjin and Hebei.
The government will fully implement the action plan for preventing and controlling air pollution, and carry out coordinated inter-regional prevention and control efforts.
The driving restriction of the eight cities in Tianjin and Hebei keep in dynamic synchronization with those in Beijing.

On February 22, 2018, in order to solve the “big city disease” in Beijing and to redistribute the function of the capital, Tianjin started to implement the new driving restriction (NDR), which allowed small and mini passenger cars with Beijing license plate to pass Tianjin.

Furthermore, apart from the vehicles whose tail number was restricted, cars with Beijing license plate could pass only within morning and evening peak: during 7 a.m. to 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. in working days, or within the outer ring road in Tianjin.
In other words, cars from Beijing were treated equally as local cars in Tianjin.
This is also in accord with what we expected from hypothesis.
Whether these appearances of phenomenon are influenced by DR or NDR remain to be further verified.

This study contributes to the existing literature in the following two ways. (1) We compare the effect of the driving restrictions in different cities, while previous studies were limited to only one city.

Thus, we explore whether there is a positive externality in the implementation of the driving restrictions. (2) This study also attempts to fill the literature gap by comparing the looser driving restriction with the previous driving restriction.
Moreover, some studies discussed the stricter traffic restriction could lead the air pollution level to increase.
Therefore, our study analyses the results of regression discontinuity to test whether weakening driving restriction could be more helpful to improve air quality.
